title: Chain rule and implicit differentiation
note: Chain rule: differentiate the outer function, keep the inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the inside: [f(g(x))]′ = f′(g(x)) · g′(x). In implicit differentiation, treat y as a function of x, so every y-term picks up a factor dy/dx.

read.title: Rates that multiply
text: Suppose u changes 3 times as fast as x, and y changes 5 times as fast as u. Then y changes 15 times as fast as x. That is the whole idea of the chain rule: when one quantity depends on another that depends on a third, rates multiply. In Leibniz notation, dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx).

In practice, spot the outer function and the inner function. For (x² + 1)³, the outer function is cubing and the inner function is x² + 1. Differentiate the outer function as if the inside were a single variable, giving 3(x² + 1)², then multiply by the inside's derivative, 2x. The result is 6x(x² + 1)². Forgetting that final factor is the most common chain-rule error.

Implicit differentiation is the chain rule applied to equations that are not solved for y. On the circle x² + y² = 25, treat y as some unknown function of x and differentiate both sides. The x² term gives 2x, and y² gives 2y · dy/dx by the chain rule. Solving 2x + 2y · dy/dx = 0 yields dy/dx = −x/y, which gives the slope at any point on the circle without ever solving for y.
